editorial:
PÃ¡l FejÅ‘s's Lonesome (Universal Pictures, 1928) follows two isolated working-class New Yorkersâ€”Jim (Glenn Tryon), a lathe operator, and Mary (Barbara Kent), a telephone switchboard operatorâ€”who meet and fall in love during a Fourth of July holiday at Coney Island, only to lose each other in the holiday crowds before discovering they are next-door neighbors. FejÅ‘s shot largely on location using a mobile camera, building the film around color tinting, superimposition, and rapid montage rather than conventional narrative continuity; three dialogue sequences were grafted on when Universal pivoted to sound, making Lonesome one of the first part-talkies. The Library of Congress selected it for the National Film Registry in 2010.

The 1928 print is free to reuse: the 95-year US copyright term expired on January 1, 2024, placing Lonesome in the same unconditional public domain category as all US works published through 1928, regardless of whether Universal filed a renewal in the 1950s. The rights trap that actually applies is the Criterion Collection's 2012 Blu-ray and DVD restoration (spine #612). Criterion's HD transfer, their reconstruction of the hand-tinted sequences, and any newly recorded musical accompaniment on the disc are independently copyrighted. A creator should source from the Internet Archive's copies of the pre-Criterion print and treat any modern audio accompaniment encountered on streaming platforms as protected until the specific license is confirmed.
faq: Is the Lonesome (1928) print in the public domain?

Yes. The 95-year US copyright term for all 1928 publications expired on January 1, 2024, placing the original Universal print in the public domain unconditionally. The Criterion Collection's 2012 restoration master is a separate, independently copyrighted work and is not free to copy or rebroadcast.
Can I freely use the dialogue or music from this film?

The original 1928 recorded sound elementsâ€”three dialogue scenes and any score or music baked into the period print, including Irving Berlin's 'Always' (itself PD, published 1925)â€”are public domain along with the film. If you are working from a modern restoration copy sourced from Criterion or a streaming platform, the audio track may include a separately copyrighted recorded accompaniment. Source from the Internet Archive's original-print copies to stay clearly within public domain.
